section_header: Why Tinnitus Is More Than Noise
audio_label: Why Tinnitus Is More Than Noise
audio_transcript: Tinnitus often feels like it is only about the sound: the ringing, buzzing, hissing, pulsing, or other noise that will not seem to turn off. That sound is real, and it can be distressing. But the experience of tinnitus is also shaped by what is happening in your body, your mind, and your daily life. This section introduces that bigger picture so the rest of the app makes sense.

audio_transcript: It is natural to focus on the sound first. When tinnitus feels loud or intrusive, it can seem like everything would be better if the sound simply disappeared. Sound matters, and sound therapy is still one of the core tools we will use. But tinnitus distress often grows when other parts of life get pulled into the cycle: poor sleep, stress, fear, frustration, avoidance, and feeling misunderstood. Looking at the whole picture gives you more places to make useful change.

audio_transcript: If tinnitus were only a hearing issue, then adding more sound would solve the whole problem. Many people do benefit from hearing aids, background sound, or other sound therapy tools, but those tools may not fully address the emotional and lifestyle impact of tinnitus. That does not mean sound therapy doesn’t work. It means tinnitus is being influenced by more than one system. The goal is not to find one perfect fix. The goal is to learn which parts of the experience you can influence, then build a plan around those levers.

section_header: Body: hearing, sound, and the nervous system
audio_label: Body: hearing, sound, and the nervous system
audio_transcript: The body side of tinnitus includes the physical and medical parts of tinnitus. This may include hearing loss, noise exposure, aging, medication effects, injury, jaw or neck factors, or changes in how the auditory system and nervous system respond to sound. Sound therapy and hearing care live here because they change what the ears and brain are receiving. If hearing loss is present, audiology care and appropriate amplification can be a major part of tinnitus management.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: The mind side of tinnitus includes your reactions to tinnitus: attention, worry, fear, frustration, self-talk, and the meaning your brain attaches to the sound. This is not saying tinnitus is imaginary. The sound is real. The point is that your reaction to the sound can make it feel more threatening, more intrusive, or harder to live with. Skills like mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, acceptance, and self-compassion all work with this part of the tinnitus experience.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Life: sleep, routines, relationships, and the world around you
audio_label: Life: sleep, routines, relationships, and the world around you
audio_transcript: The life side of tinnitus includes the ways tinnitus changes your day-to-day routines and relationships. You might avoid quiet rooms, skip social events, struggle at work, feel misunderstood, or notice that sleep becomes more stressful. These are not small side issues. They are part of how tinnitus becomes dominant. Communication skills, sleep education, sound planning, and gradual re-engagement help you keep your life from shrinking around tinnitus.

audio_transcript: Multimodal simply means using more than one type of tool. Sound therapy can help with the sound environment. Mindfulness can help with attention. Distress tolerance can help with difficult moments. Cognitive reframing can help with thoughts that jump too far too fast. Sleep tools, self-compassion, and communication skills can help with the parts of life that tinnitus disrupts. No single tool has to do everything. Each tool gives you another way to influence the experience.

audio_transcript: This app is a guided educational companion. You can read, listen, practice, and come back to sections when you need them. The best way to begin is to understand the big picture, then start with sound therapy because it is often the most concrete first step. From there, the other sections build tools for attention, difficult moments, thoughts, sleep, self-support, and communication. You do not need to master everything at once.

audio_transcript: Self-guided tools can be powerful, but they are not always easy to apply on your own. If you feel like you need individual help, feel confused, stuck, unsafe, or overwhelmed, support from an audiologist, ENT, mental health professional, sleep specialist, or other qualified clinician may be important. Getting help is not a failure. It is one of the ways people make these tools easier to use and more specific to their own situation.

audio_transcript: Using these skills takes effort, and that can feel discouraging when tinnitus is already stressful. The goal is not to do everything perfectly. The goal is to test small strategies, notice what helps, and build a plan that gives you more influence over your day. Consistent sound use, gentle habit changes, a calmer response to thoughts, and short moments of mindfulness can all become evidence that tinnitus does not have to dominate every part of life.

audio_transcript: Before you start learning tools, take a moment to name your reason for being here. Are you looking for relief, understanding, better sleep, more confidence, or a way to make everyday life feel easier? Then imagine six months from now. How would you want tinnitus to feel different, not only in sound, but in how it affects your experience? Finally, choose one small step you can take this week. Naming your why can make the rest of the work feel more connected to your life.

audio_transcript: This exercise helps you sort your tinnitus experience into three areas. Body includes physical or medical factors, such as hearing changes, sound sensitivity, injury, or other health issues. Mind includes thoughts, emotions, stress, and worry. Life includes routines, sleep, relationships, work, and environments. A few words in each area is enough. The purpose is not to diagnose yourself. The purpose is to see the whole picture and identify where a useful next step might be.

audio_label: Main points before you move on
audio_transcript: Tinnitus is more than sound. The sound matters, but stress, attention, sleep, thoughts, avoidance, and social life can all change how tinnitus feels. Looking at tinnitus through Body, Mind, and Life gives you more than one place to intervene. This app can be used on your own, but professional support can help when the skills feel difficult or when medical, hearing, sleep, or mental health concerns need attention. section_header: Using helpful sounds to manage tinnitus
audio_label: Using helpful sounds to manage tinnitus
audio_transcript:
Sound therapy means using comfortable outside sound to make tinnitus less dominant in your listening environment. The goal is not to blast tinnitus away or prove that you can ignore it. The goal is to give your ears and brain another sound to work with so tinnitus can gradually become less central.

This is often one of the most practical starting points in tinnitus management because it works directly with the sound experience. When sound therapy is used consistently and comfortably, it can help set the stage for the other skills in this app, including acceptance, mindfulness, distress tolerance, cognitive reframing, and sleep support.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: What you will learn in this section
audio_label: What you will learn in this section
audio_transcript:
By the end of this section, you should understand why sound therapy can help the brain get used to tinnitus, how to choose sounds and devices that feel comfortable, and how to set the volume so tinnitus and sound therapy gently overlap.

The most important skill is finding the right volume level. Sound that is too quiet will not help much, while sound that completely covers tinnitus may become a form of avoidance. The useful range is where the sound therapy is clearly present, but tinnitus is not being pushed out of awareness entirely.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
When tinnitus is the only noticeable sound, the brain may treat it as the most important thing in the room. Sound therapy changes that listening environment. By adding a neutral or soothing background sound, you reduce the contrast between silence and tinnitus.

Over time, this can help the brain treat tinnitus as a lower-priority signal. It may still be there, but it does not have to take center stage or pull your attention as strongly. This process is gradual, and it works best when sound therapy is used patiently and consistently.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Sound therapy means adding soft, steady, or soothing sound to your environment. This might come from a fan, a sound machine, a phone app, a speaker, open-ear headphones, or hearing aids. The sound does not have to be special or complicated. It just needs to be comfortable and useful for you.

Think of sound therapy as an auditory backdrop. The outside sound gives your brain something else to hear, so tinnitus is not standing alone in silence. The aim is not to erase tinnitus in the moment, but to make the listening environment easier for your brain to handle.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
A simple way to understand sound therapy is to imagine sitting in a restaurant. Music, voices, and movement do not erase every small sound in the room, but they help those sounds blend into the background. The clink of silverware may still happen, but it usually does not demand your full attention.

Tinnitus can work in a similar way. When the room is completely quiet, tinnitus may feel isolated and intense. When gentle sound is added, tinnitus may still be present, but it has more competition and can begin to feel less intrusive.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Why silence can make tinnitus feel louder
audio_label: Why silence can make tinnitus feel louder
audio_transcript:
Many people notice tinnitus most strongly in quiet. That does not necessarily mean tinnitus has become more dangerous or permanently louder. It may mean there is less outside sound competing for attention.

Sound therapy reduces the stark contrast between silence and tinnitus. That can lower the feeling that tinnitus is the only thing happening. For some people this helps with concentration, relaxation, evening routines, and sleep preparation. It also gives the brain repeated opportunities to learn that tinnitus can be present without needing an alarm response.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Masking is not the same as sound therapy
audio_label: Masking is not the same as sound therapy
audio_transcript:
Many people use the word masking to mean any use of sound for tinnitus, but full masking and sound therapy are not the same thing. Full masking means turning sound up until tinnitus is completely covered. That can be useful for a short break or a high-distress moment, but it is not the main goal of sound therapy, as we discuss it here.

Sound therapy usually works best when it supports adaptation. That means the sound is comfortable and present, while tinnitus may still be partly audible. In that volume range, the brain can begin learning that tinnitus does not need to dominate or trigger constant monitoring.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Full masking can feel good because it gives immediate relief from hearing tinnitus. The limitation is that the relief often stops when the masking sound stops. If the brain only learns that tinnitus must be hidden, tinnitus may feel more threatening when it returns.

A habituation-oriented sound therapy approach is different. It allows some awareness of tinnitus while adding a steady, supportive sound. This can help the brain learn that tinnitus is present but not urgent. That learning is usually slower than short-term masking, but it is often more useful for daily management.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Finding the sound therapy sweet spot
audio_label: Finding the sound therapy sweet spot
audio_transcript:
The sound therapy sweet spot is the range where you can hear both the sound therapy and your tinnitus. If the sound therapy is too quiet, it may not give your brain enough input to work with. If it is too loud and completely covers tinnitus, it may become more about escaping the sound than adapting to it.

The middle volume range is usually the most helpful. In that range, tinnitus is present, but it is not alone. Sound therapy becomes a calm companion to your listening environment rather than a battle to overpower tinnitus.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
The bottom zone is too quiet: the sound therapy is not audible enough to help. The top zone is too loud: the sound covers tinnitus completely, which may be useful briefly but is not the main long-term goal.

The middle zone is the target. You can hear the sound therapy and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap gives the brain a chance to practice hearing tinnitus without treating it as the only sound that matters.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Habituation means the brain adapts and becomes less reactive to a repeated stimulus. When habituation happens with tinnitus, you may still notice tinnitus if you listen for it, but it no longer creates the same stress or urgency.

Sound therapy means using gentle background sound to reduce the impact of tinnitus and support habituation. An external sound source is any device or method that delivers that sound, such as a fan, speaker, phone app, sound machine, hearing aids, or open-ear headphones.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
There is no perfect sound for everyone. Some people like rain, ocean waves, crickets, fans, white noise, pink noise, gentle music, or other steady sounds. Some people like sounds that another person would find irritating. If it helps you and you can use it comfortably, it can be a good sound for you.

The best starting point is to try a few neutral or pleasant sounds and notice which ones feel comfortable or soothing. If a sound becomes annoying, you are not doing anything wrong. Try a different sound or change the setting.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Sound therapy can come from many places: a phone app, small speaker, sound machine, fan, open-ear headphones, bone-conduction headphones, or hearing aids. The right device depends on where you are, what you are doing, and what feels comfortable.

If you have hearing loss, hearing care deserves special attention. Hearing aids can act like a highly personalized form of sound therapy by restoring sounds the brain has been missing. For many people with hearing loss and tinnitus, addressing hearing directly is one of the most useful starting points.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Start with the sound low. Slowly raise it until you can hear the sound therapy clearly. Then notice whether tinnitus is still partly present. If you cannot hear the sound therapy, it is too low. If tinnitus disappears completely, the sound may be louder than you need for everyday sound therapy.

Aim for a comfortable overlap. You should be aware of the support sound, and you may still notice tinnitus, but neither one should feel like it is taking over. The exact level may change from day to day, and that is okay.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Using sound therapy during the day
audio_label: Using sound therapy during the day
audio_transcript:
Sound therapy is often most useful during quiet tasks or times when tinnitus tends to grab your attention. You might use it while reading, doing work around the home, working at a desk, relaxing in the evening, or preparing for bed.

Consistency matters more than perfection. You do not need to analyze every minute. The goal is to give your brain repeated, comfortable exposure to a richer sound environment so tinnitus becomes less dominant over time.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Many people notice tinnitus more at night because the environment is quieter and there are fewer distractions. Gentle sound at night can make the transition toward sleep feel less like a direct confrontation with tinnitus.

This does not mean sound therapy is a full sleep treatment. It is one supportive tool. If sleep is a persistent problem, or if there are signs of a sleep condition such as sleep apnea, that deserves proper evaluation. But for many people, a comfortable background sound can make bedtime feel less stark and less silent.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: How sound therapy supports the rest of the app
audio_label: How sound therapy supports the rest of the app
audio_transcript:
Sound therapy is the main auditory tool in this app, but it works best as part of a bigger approach. Comfortable sound can make mindfulness easier, support distress tolerance, reduce the feeling of being trapped in silence, and give you a better environment for practicing acceptance and cognitive reframing.

That is why sound therapy appears in more than one place. It is not just a sound tool. It is a foundation that can support emotional regulation, attention flexibility, sleep routines, and everyday re-engagement.

audio_transcript:
Tinnitus and sound sensitivity often travel together. If ordinary sound feels sharp, uncomfortable, or threatening, it can be tempting to avoid sound as much as possible. That reaction makes sense, but living in a quieter and quieter world can sometimes keep the sound system on high alert.

For sound sensitivity, the same basic principle still applies: comfortable, controlled sound can help the system feel safer over time. The key is not to push into volume levels that are uncomfortable or painful. Start gently, stay below the point of sensitivity, and use sounds that feel enjoyable or neutral.

audio_transcript:
One simple sound-sensitivity practice is to use enjoyable music on speakers for 10 to 15 minutes. Start with the volume all the way down. Slowly raise it until you begin to notice sensitivity, then lower it slightly below that point. Listen only if it feels comfortable.

The purpose is not to tolerate bothersome sound levels. The purpose is to give your brain and body a controlled sound experience where nothing bad happens. If the level changes from day to day, treat that information non-judgmentally.

section_header: FAQ: How loud should sound therapy be?
audio_label: FAQ: How loud should sound therapy be?
audio_transcript:
A useful starting point is just below the level where sound therapy would completely cover tinnitus. You want to hear the support sound and still have some awareness of tinnitus. That overlap is what makes it sound therapy rather than simply blocking tinnitus out.

There may be moments when fuller masking is useful for a short break. For daily management, though, the balanced volume level is usually the better target.

section_header: FAQ: Does the type of sound matter?
audio_label: FAQ: Does the type of sound matter?
audio_transcript:
The type of sound matters mostly because you need to be able to use it comfortably. Nature sounds, steady noise, fan sounds, gentle music, crickets, or water sounds can all be reasonable options.

The best sound is not the one someone else calls perfect. It is the one that works for your ears, your environment, and your nervous system on that day.

section_header: FAQ: Will sound therapy get rid of tinnitus?
audio_label: FAQ: Will sound therapy get rid of tinnitus?
audio_transcript:
Sound therapy is not a promise that tinnitus will disappear. The more realistic goal is that tinnitus becomes less dominant, less threatening, and easier to live with.

Many people find that sound therapy helps reduce distress even when tinnitus is still present. That distinction is important: improvement can mean a better relationship with tinnitus, not only a change in the sound itself.

audio_label: FAQ: When should I use sound therapy?
audio_transcript:
Use sound therapy when it helps you stay engaged with your life. That might mean quiet work, reading, relaxing, evening routines, or getting ready for sleep. The goal is not to become dependent on sound every moment of the day.

Use it as support. If you notice that you are using sound only to avoid ever hearing tinnitus, return to the sweet spot idea and the Acceptance and Change section.

Sound therapy adds comfortable outside sound so tinnitus is not alone in silence. The sound should usually be audible but not overpowering. Consistency matters, and the sound you choose should be something you can use comfortably over time.

Sound therapy is also more powerful when it is combined with the rest of tinnitus management. It can support mindfulness, distress tolerance, sleep routines, cognitive reframing, and a more flexible relationship with tinnitus.

Before you leave this section, choose one small way you could use sound therapy this week. Keep it simple: one sound, one device, one situation. You can always adjust later.

It also helps to write a reminder to be patient with yourself. Sound therapy is a learning process. Some days will be easier than others, and needing to adjust the sound does not mean you are failing. It means you are listening and responding.

audio_label: Sound safety and when to seek help
audio_transcript:
Use comfortable sound. Do not push into painful volume. If sound sensitivity is severe, worsening, or interfering with daily life, professional guidance can help. If you have hearing loss, sudden hearing changes, one-sided symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, dizziness, neurological symptoms, or other medical concerns, consider appropriate hearing healthcare or medical evaluation.

This app teaches sound therapy as an educational self-management tool. It does not replace audiology, ENT, mental health care, sleep medicine, or emergency care when those are needed.

section_header: Acceptance and change can work together
audio_label: Acceptance and change can work together
audio_transcript:
When tinnitus feels difficult, it is natural to want it gone. That reaction makes sense. The problem is that tinnitus does not always respond to force, and the harder you fight to make it disappear in a single moment, the more your attention and energy can become wrapped around it.

Acceptance does not mean giving up. In this section, acceptance means acknowledging what is happening right now so you can use your energy more wisely. Change means taking practical steps that reduce distress, support daily life, and help you stay connected to what matters.

audio_transcript: By the end of this section, you should be able to tell the difference between acceptance and giving up, recognize how avoidance can make tinnitus more frustrating, describe how acceptance and change can happen at the same time, and practice at least one acceptance-based exercise for tinnitus-related stress.

section_header: Pause and reflect: what happened last time?
audio_label: Pause and reflect: what happened last time?
audio_transcript:
Think about a recent moment when tinnitus made you angry, upset, or tense. What did you do to handle that feeling? Did your response lower the stress, or did it keep the struggle going?

Now ask one small question: if I had accepted that tinnitus was present in that moment, stoping the fight against it without liking it or approving of it, what might have felt different?

section_header: Acceptance means noticing what is here
audio_label: Acceptance means noticing what is here
audio_transcript:
Acceptance means allowing yourself to notice that tinnitus is present without spending all your energy trying to erase it. It does not mean you like tinnitus. It does not mean you want it to stay. It does not mean you believe nothing can improve.

It means you are starting from reality: tinnitus is here right now, and the next useful step probably will not come from arguing with that fact.

section_header: Change means acting where you have influence
audio_label: Change means acting where you have influence
audio_transcript:
Change means taking active steps to improve your life and reduce distress. That might mean using sound therapy, asking for support, practicing mindfulness, communicating a need, or returning to an activity tinnitus has pushed aside.

Change does not have to mean forcing tinnitus to disappear. It can mean making today more workable, your environment more supportive, and your reactions less controlled by the sound.

audio_transcript:
Many people hear the word acceptance and think it means throwing in the towel. That is not what we mean here.

Resignation says, “Nothing can change, so why try?” Acceptance says, “This is the situation I am in right now, and I can still choose the next useful step.” Acceptance is active. It helps you stop fighting the impossible in this moment so you can put effort into something that may actually help.

section_header: Why trying only to eliminate tinnitus can backfire
audio_label: Why trying only to eliminate tinnitus can backfire
audio_transcript:
At the beginning, many people put all their energy into making tinnitus vanish. They may avoid quiet places, stop doing things they enjoy, search constantly for cures, or feel crushed whenever a treatment does not work right away.

Those reactions are understandable. But when your whole life becomes organized around eliminating tinnitus, tinnitus can become even more central. The struggle itself starts taking up the space that your routines, relationships, hobbies, and rest used to occupy.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript:
Avoidance can bring short-term relief. Masking tinnitus fully, leaving a quiet room, canceling plans, or checking the internet again may feel like it lowers distress for a moment. The problem is that avoidance can also teach the brain that tinnitus is something you cannot face.

Over time, the world may get smaller. Acceptance helps reverse that pattern by asking, “What can I allow for this moment, and what useful action can I take anyway?”

section_header: Sound therapy shows acceptance and change together
audio_label: Sound therapy shows acceptance and change together
audio_transcript:
Sound therapy is a good example of acceptance and change working together. If you use sound only to cover tinnitus completely all day, the purpose becomes escape. That may help briefly, but it can also keep the brain from learning that tinnitus is safe enough to tune out.

When sound therapy is set in the middle volume range, where you can hear the support sound and may still notice tinnitus, you are accepting enough of the sound for the brain to learn while still changing the environment to make it easier to tolerate.

audio_transcript:
The Yes AND mindset comes from the idea that two truths can exist at the same time. You can acknowledge tinnitus honestly and still take a useful next step.

For example: “Yes, my tinnitus is tough today, and I can use a gentle background sound while I get ready.” Or, “Yes, I wish this were different, and I can still go to dinner with friends.” The first half is acceptance. The second half is change.

section_header: Two truths can sit next to each other
audio_label: Two truths can sit next to each other
audio_transcript:
Without this kind of both-and thinking, tinnitus can push you toward all-or-nothing choices: either I fix this completely, or my life is ruined. That trap is exhausting.

A more balanced view says: tinnitus can be present, and I can still take care of myself. I can dislike this sound, and I can still choose something meaningful. I can want improvement, and I can stop demanding that everything change before I live my life.

audio_transcript:
Imagine tinnitus on the other side of a rope in a tug of war. You pull harder and harder, trying to win. But the more you pull, the more tired and stuck you become.

Pulling the rope might look like masking tinnitus every moment, avoiding quiet places, arguing with the sound in your mind, or searching for answers long after the search has stopped helping. The question is not whether those reactions make sense. They do, and are reasonable things to do at first. The question is whether staying in the tug-of-war is giving you your life back.

section_header: What would dropping the rope mean?
audio_label: What would dropping the rope mean?
audio_transcript:
Dropping the rope does not mean tinnitus wins. It does not mean you like tinnitus or accept that nothing can improve. It means you stop spending this moment on a fight that is not helping.

When you drop the rope, even briefly, you may have more energy for something else: using a coping tool, changing the room, resting, connecting with someone, or returning to an activity that matters.

audio_transcript: Acceptance means embracing the present experience without spending all your energy suppressing it, fighting it, or denying it. It acknowledges what you cannot fully change right now and frees mental energy for more constructive actions.

audio_transcript: Change means taking active steps to enhance your well-being. That may include coping tools, goals, problem-solving, sound therapy, communication, or daily routines. Change focuses on what can improve, even when tinnitus is still present.

Taking acceptance and change into real life begins with noticing when you are locked in battle. Are you telling yourself, “I will only be okay when this goes away”? Are you organizing the day around avoiding tinnitus?

When tinnitus feels overwhelming, it can shrink your world. You may avoid hobbies, social opportunities, music, work tasks, quiet rooms, or routines that used to matter.

section_header: Mindfulness: finding calm in the present moment
audio_label: Mindfulness: finding calm in the present moment
audio_transcript: Mindfulness means learning to notice what is happening right now without immediately fighting it, avoiding it, or judging it. For tinnitus, this does not mean liking the ringing or pretending it is pleasant. It means practicing the ability to notice tinnitus as one part of the moment, alongside your breath, body, thoughts, emotions, and the sounds around you.

audio_label: What you will practice in this section
audio_transcript: In this section, you will learn what mindfulness is, how it differs from simple relaxation, and why it can be useful when tinnitus feels intrusive. audio_transcript: Mindfulness is the practice of being fully present with your experiences, including thoughts, feelings, sensations, and sounds, without trying to push away discomfort or cling tightly to comfort. With tinnitus, this means gently noticing the ringing, buzzing, or hissing while also noticing the rest of the room, the body, the breath, and the activity you are doing. The skill is not to force tinnitus away. The skill is to widen attention so tinnitus is no longer the only thing your mind is holding.

section_header: You do not have to like the ringing
audio_label: You do not have to like the ringing
audio_transcript: A key idea in this section is that you do not have to like tinnitus for mindfulness to help. You are not trying to convince yourself that the sound is pleasant. You are practicing a less combative way of noticing it. When the mind stops treating tinnitus as an emergency every time it appears, the sound can begin to lose some of its emotional force.

audio_transcript: Many people assume mindfulness means sitting silently for a long time and focusing on tinnitus. That misunderstanding can make mindfulness feel impossible. In this app, mindfulness is much broader. It can be one breath before you check your phone, a minute of noticing sounds during a walk, or a short pause while holding a warm drink. Silence is not required. Everyday sounds can become anchors for awareness.

section_header: Mindfulness is not the same as relaxation
audio_label: Mindfulness is not the same as relaxation
audio_transcript: Mindfulness and relaxation often overlap, but they are not the same thing. Relaxation focuses on feeling calmer. Mindfulness focuses on noticing what is here with more steadiness and less judgment. Sometimes mindfulness will help you feel relaxed. Other times, it simply helps you notice stress, tinnitus, or frustration without reacting as quickly.

audio_transcript: When tinnitus appears, the mind may quickly label it as awful, unbearable, or a sign that the day is ruined. Mindfulness gives you a different option: notice the sound and notice the reaction to the sound. You might silently label it, “ringing,” “thought,” or “frustration.” This does not erase tinnitus, but it creates a small pause between the sound and the reaction.

audio_transcript: Tinnitus often becomes more distressing when the sound is paired with alarm, fear, self-blame, or catastrophic thoughts. Mindfulness-based approaches help by lowering emotional reactivity. Instead of automatically moving from “I hear tinnitus” to “I can’t stand this,” you practice noticing the sound, taking a breath, and letting the moment be larger than the tinnitus alone.

section_header: Mindfulness can work with sound therapy
audio_label: Mindfulness can work with sound therapy
audio_transcript: Sound therapy can make mindfulness more accessible. Gentle background sound gives your attention something neutral to notice, especially when silence makes tinnitus feel too sharp. Mindfulness then helps you use sound therapy without making it another form of panic or avoidance. Together, they support the same goal: helping tinnitus become less dominant in your awareness.

audio_transcript: The acceptance section focused on dropping the struggle long enough to choose a useful next step. Mindfulness is how you practice that in real time. When you become aware of tinnitus, you can notice it, feel the urge to fight it, and choose where your attention goes next. This is not passive. It is active training in how you respond.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: The 3-2-1 senses practice is a simple way to widen attention. Look around and name three things you can see. Then identify two sounds or auditory sensations you can notice. Finally, notice one physical sensation, such as your feet on the floor or clothing against your skin. Pause for a moment afterward and ask whether your awareness or mood shifted.

audio_transcript: Mindfulness means paying attention, on purpose, to the present moment without judging what you notice as good or bad. Present-moment awareness means focusing on right now instead of replaying past difficult moments or jumping into future what-ifs. Non-judgment means approaching the experience with openness rather than immediately labeling it awful, unbearable, or your fault.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Mindfulness does not need to be saved for a special meditation session. You can practice it in small moments: before checking your phone, while sitting down, while walking, or when tinnitus first grabs your attention. If tinnitus appears, acknowledge it gently: “I hear that ringing.” Then expand attention to the body, the room, the breath, or the activity in front of you.

audio_transcript: A mindful pause gives you a moment to respond rather than react. That pause may be one breath, one label, or one shift of attention. The goal is not to make tinnitus disappear in that moment. The goal is to keep the sound from automatically deciding your mood, your behavior, or the next hour of your day.

section_header: How mindfulness connects to the bigger picture
audio_label: How mindfulness connects to the bigger picture
audio_transcript: Mindfulness, similar to sound therapy, supports many of the other tools in this app. It strengthens acceptance by helping you observe tinnitus without immediate resistance. It supports sound therapy by helping you stay flexible whether background sound is present or not. It supports distress tolerance by giving you a pause button in difficult moments, and it supports cognitive reframing by helping you see thoughts as events in the mind rather than facts that must be obeyed.

audio_label: FAQ: Will mindfulness make me focus on tinnitus more?
audio_transcript: At first, mindfulness may make you more aware of tinnitus because you are practicing noticing. That does not mean you are doing it wrong. The goal is to notice tinnitus alongside other experiences, not to stare at it mentally. With practice, awareness becomes broader and tinnitus tends to have less control over the whole moment.

audio_transcript: No. Mindfulness can happen with traffic, fans, appliances, conversation, music, or sound therapy in the background. Everyday sound can help anchor attention. Tinnitus can be included in awareness without becoming the only sound that matters.

audio_transcript: Mindfulness and relaxation can overlap, but mindfulness is broader. You may feel calmer, but the main skill is learning to observe your experience and let go of harsh judgments. Sometimes you will practice mindfulness during a calm moment. Other times you will practice it while you are uncomfortable.

audio_label: FAQ: How long do I need to practice?
audio_transcript: You do not need to meditate for long periods every day for mindfulness to matter. Short, frequent practices can build the same kind of skill. One breath, one minute of listening, or a brief 3-2-1 senses check-in can be enough to practice returning to the present moment.

section_header: Exercise: Mindful Listening in Everyday Activity
audio_label: Exercise: Mindful Listening in Everyday Activity
audio_transcript: Mindful Listening helps you practice broad awareness during something ordinary, such as washing dishes, walking, or sitting with a cup of tea. Begin the activity with a slow breath. Notice all the sounds you can hear: water, footsteps, traffic, birds, the hum of a room, and tinnitus if it is present. If you notice tinnitus, label it neutrally as “ringing,” then gently widen attention to the rest of the sound environment.

audio_transcript: After a minute or two, pause and ask what changed. Did noticing other sounds shift your experience of tinnitus? Did your body or mood feel any different before and after the practice? There is no perfect answer. The point is to notice whether attention can widen, even briefly.

audio_transcript: Sound Shifting trains attention to move instead of getting locked onto one sound. Set a short timer for two to five minutes. Begin by gently noticing tinnitus for 15 to 20 seconds. Notice thoughts or feelings that arise, and label them simply as “thought” or “feeling.” Then shift attention to another sound, such as a fan, traffic, music, or your breathing. Continue moving back and forth in short intervals.

audio_transcript: When the timer ends, ask how it felt to switch your attention on purpose. Did any emotions shift during the exercise? Did tinnitus feel different after attention moved away and returned? The goal is not to like tinnitus. The goal is to practice directing awareness rather than feeling stuck.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Stay neutral when frustration appears. You can mentally note “frustration”, feel it, and try not to suppress it, and then continue. Keep the practice short at first; two or three rounds may be enough. As you become more comfortable, you can lengthen the timer or include more external sounds. You are building flexibility, not testing endurance.

audio_transcript: Sometimes mindfulness will feel difficult, especially if tinnitus is loud or you are already distressed. That does not mean mindfulness is wrong for you. Make the practice smaller. Add comfortable sound. Use 3-2-1 senses instead of a longer exercise. If you feel overwhelmed, switch to distress tolerance tools first and come back to mindfulness later.

audio_transcript: Mindfulness helps you notice tinnitus without being ruled by it. It is not about erasing the sound, but changing the response to it. Short, regular practices can interrupt thought loops and support tools like sound therapy, acceptance, distress tolerance, and cognitive reframing. Being present can reduce fear when tinnitus changes or feels louder.

audio_transcript: Distress tolerance is about what to do when tinnitus suddenly feels overwhelming. These skills are not meant to erase tinnitus or solve the whole problem in one move. Their purpose is to help you stay grounded, slow the spiral, and avoid reacting in a way that makes the moment harder. When tinnitus feels like it is pulling all of your attention, distress tolerance gives you a short-term bridge back to steadier thinking.

section_header: What you will learn in this section
audio_label: What you will learn in this section
audio_transcript: In this section, you will learn quick skills you can use when tinnitus feels intense. You will practice naming a fluctuation without assuming it is permanent, pausing before reacting, using your body to calm your nervous system, and choosing a response that supports your long-term well-being. The goal is not to never feel distress. The goal is to have a plan for what to do when distress shows up.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Distress tolerance focuses on managing emotional overwhelm in the short term. This matters for tinnitus because sudden changes in loudness, pitch, or intrusiveness can trigger panic, frustration, or a rush to do something drastic. In those moments, trying to force tinnitus away can make your attention narrow even more. Distress tolerance gives you a way to lower the intensity of the moment first, so you can decide what to do next with a clearer mind.

section_header: Why panic makes tinnitus feel bigger
audio_label: Why panic makes tinnitus feel bigger
audio_transcript: When you feel panicked about tinnitus, your brain pays closer attention to the sound. That extra attention can make tinnitus feel louder, sharper, or more threatening, even if the signal itself has not changed much. Distress tolerance interrupts this loop. A cold splash of water, a pause, a breath, or a short movement break gives your body another high-priority signal and gives your mind a chance to stop chasing the alarm.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Use the word fluctuation, not spike
audio_label: Use the word fluctuation, not spike
audio_transcript: Language matters. The word spike can make a tinnitus change sound like a permanent emergency. The word fluctuation is more neutral. It reminds you that tinnitus can move up and down, shift in tone, and feel more or less intrusive depending on the day, the body, stress, sleep, attention, and environment. A difficult fluctuation can still be unpleasant, but naming it as a fluctuation helps reduce the automatic fear that it will stay this way forever.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Distress tolerance is a short-term safety valve
audio_label: Distress tolerance is a short-term safety valve
audio_transcript: Distress tolerance is different from longer-term tools like cognitive reframing or acceptance work. It does not try to change your core beliefs about tinnitus in the middle of a hard moment. It gives you a safety valve. Once your body and mind are less activated, then you can decide whether to use sound therapy, mindfulness, a thought record, a communication skill, or simply return to what you were doing.

section_header: When distress becomes a safety concern
audio_label: When distress becomes a safety concern
audio_transcript: Distress tolerance skills are useful for intense tinnitus distress, but they are not a crisis plan. If you feel unsafe, feel at risk of harming yourself, or are in a mental health crisis, do not rely on this app as your only support. Seek immediate help through emergency services, crisis resources, or a qualified professional. These skills can be part of a broader plan, but safety comes first.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: A few terms will come up throughout this section. Distress tolerance means using skills to cope with intense emotions in the short term without making the situation worse. STOP is a quick pause-and-choose skill. TIPP is a group of body-based tools that can lower emotional intensity. Fluctuation is a neutral word for tinnitus changes, reminding you that a difficult sound moment is not automatically a permanent escalation.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: The STOP skill gives you a way to insert a pause between noticing tinnitus distress and reacting to it. Stop. Take a step back. Observe what is happening in your body, thoughts, emotions, and urges. Then proceed mindfully by choosing a response that supports you. STOP is useful because tinnitus distress often grows when the first reaction takes over before you have a chance to think.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: TIPP: use the body to calm the mind
audio_label: TIPP: use the body to calm the mind
audio_transcript: TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense movement, Paced breathing, and Paired muscle relaxation. These skills target the body’s stress response. When tinnitus distress pushes you into fight-or-flight mode, changing your physical state can help your mind come back online. The goal is not pain, exhaustion, or pushing your body too hard. The goal is safe, noticeable body-based regulation.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Distress tolerance works best when you practice it before the hardest moment. Try STOP when you feel impatient in traffic. Practice paced breathing when you are mildly stressed. Notice what happens when you use cold water or a short movement break during a smaller frustration. Rehearsing these skills in ordinary moments makes them easier to find when tinnitus feels much more intense.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: From “fix this now” to “I can handle this moment”
audio_label: From “fix this now” to “I can handle this moment”
audio_transcript: A difficult tinnitus moment can create the feeling that something must be fixed immediately. Distress tolerance shifts the goal. Instead of demanding that tinnitus disappear right now, the goal becomes: I can handle this moment without making it worse. That shift matters. It lets you take the next useful step, whether that is sound therapy, a walk, a breathing practice, a call to someone supportive, or returning to an activity you care about.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Temperature can pull attention back into the body quickly. One simple version is holding a small ice cube for a short time and noticing the cold, the water, and the changing sensation. The goal is not pain. The goal is to give your nervous system a clear, safe, high-priority sensation so your mind has a moment to step out of the tinnitus spiral. If it becomes painful or unsafe, stop.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Another sensory option: frozen orange grounding
audio_label: Another sensory option: frozen orange grounding
audio_transcript: Some people like a sensory grounding object that changes over time. A frozen orange can offer cold, texture, scent, and movement as it warms in your hand. You might notice frost, the peel, the citrus smell, or the way the surface softens. This can feel like a strange suggestion, but it gets your mind out of focusing on tinnitus. It is simply another way to give attention a safe, concrete place to land when tinnitus-related thoughts are spinning.

section_header: Exercise: Take a pause before reacting
audio_label: Exercise: Take a pause before reacting
audio_transcript: When tinnitus fluctuates, it is easy to react immediately with frustration or panic. The STOP exercise helps you pause, assess what is happening, and choose a response that is more likely to help. Instead of being caught in the first automatic reaction, you give yourself a few seconds of space. That space can be enough to keep the moment from becoming larger than it needs to be.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Start by mentally saying “Stop.” Then take a step back, either by changing your posture, taking a breath, or briefly moving to another space. Observe what is happening in your body and mind: emotions, thoughts, physical sensations, and urges. Then proceed mindfully. Ask, what response will help me in the long term? That might mean using a skill, continuing your activity, or choosing a small supportive action.

section_header: Exercise: Use your body to calm your mind
audio_label: Exercise: Use your body to calm your mind
audio_transcript: When tinnitus distress is high, your body may act as if there is a threat. Your heart may race, your breathing may change, and your attention may lock onto the sound. TIPP skills work through the body. They do not argue with the mind. They change the physical state enough to help you feel more in control.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Temperature means using a safe, noticeable temperature change to shift the body’s stress response. You might splash cool water on your face, hold a cool cloth, or briefly place your hands in cool water. The goal is not to cause pain through the cold. The goal is to create a strong enough sensation that your body and mind pause the alarm loop.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Intense movement means a brief burst of safe physical activity, such as marching in place, a few squats, jumping jacks, or a short walk. This is not a workout plan and it is not appropriate for every body or every situation. The idea is to burn off some stress energy and help the nervous system reset. Choose an option that is safe for you.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Paced breathing slows the rhythm of the body. One simple pattern is to breathe in for about four seconds and breathe out for six to eight seconds. The longer exhale helps signal that your body does not need to stay in full alarm mode. You do not have to make the breath perfect. A few slower breaths can be enough to create a little space.

audio_transcript: Paired muscle relaxation means gently tensing and releasing a muscle group while pairing the release with a slower breath. You might raise your shoulders slightly, hold for a few seconds, and then let them drop as you exhale. The contrast between tension and release can help your body recognize that it does not need to stay braced.

section_header: How distress tolerance connects to the bigger picture
audio_label: How distress tolerance connects to the bigger picture
audio_transcript: Distress tolerance sits between mindfulness and cognitive reframing. Mindfulness helps you notice what is happening. Distress tolerance helps when the intensity is too high to think clearly. Once the tornado slows down, cognitive reframing can help you look at the thoughts that made the moment feel even worse. This section also connects to acceptance: even if you cannot change tinnitus right now, you can change how you respond to the moment.

audio_label: FAQ: Will these skills make tinnitus quieter?
audio_transcript: Distress tolerance skills do not directly change the tinnitus sound. Their job is to lower the emotional reaction that makes the sound feel unmanageable. When the body and mind are less alarmed, tinnitus may feel less dominating, even if the sound itself is still present.

audio_transcript: That is common. Skills are hardest to remember when distress is highest. Practice them during smaller frustrations so they become familiar. audio_transcript: Cognitive behavioral therapy often describes a loop between what we think, how we feel, and what we do. With tinnitus, the loop might start with noticing the sound. That leads to a thought such as, “Today is going to be terrible.” That thought creates dread, and the dread may lead you to cancel plans, check tinnitus repeatedly, or search for a quick fix. audio_transcript: Think of cognitive restructuring as reality-checking your mind. First, identify the distressing thought. For example, “This ringing is awful, so my day is ruined” might become, “This moment is difficult, and I have had difficult tinnitus moments before without the entire day being lost.”

audio_transcript: Cognitive restructuring is not about telling yourself that tinnitus is wonderful or that everything is fine. audio_transcript: Cognitive reframing may not change the tinnitus itself. Instead, it changes the stress loop around the sound. audio_transcript: Cognitive distortions are common thinking shortcuts. They are not signs that you are doing something wrong; they are patterns to notice. With tinnitus, it may sound like, “People think I am overreacting.” Sometimes people may not understand, but that is different from knowing what they think. section_header: Sleep and tinnitus can affect each other

audio_transcript: Many people with tinnitus notice that nighttime can feel harder. Life is quieter, the day is over, and there may be fewer distractions from the sound. At the same time, poor sleep can make the next day feel heavier, increasing stress, frustration, and tinnitus distress. This section helps you understand that two-way relationship and gives you practical sleep-supportive steps without turning this app into a sleep-treatment program.

audio_label: What you will learn in this section

section_header: Why sleep belongs in tinnitus management
audio_label: Why sleep belongs in tinnitus management
audio_transcript: Sleep may seem separate from tinnitus, but the two are often closely connected. When sleep is poor, your stress system has less time to recover, your attention may narrow, and difficult sounds can feel harder to ignore. When tinnitus feels threatening at bedtime, sleep can become harder to reach. That is why sleep belongs in a multimodal tinnitus plan.

audio_transcript: A difficult night can lead to fatigue, irritability, and more worry the next day. That stress can make tinnitus feel more intrusive, especially when you are tired. Then, when bedtime returns, the memory of the previous bad night can make you anxious before you even lie down. This loop can feel powerful, but it also gives you several places to intervene.

section_header: Why quiet nights can feel harder
audio_label: Why quiet nights can feel harder
audio_transcript: Tinnitus often stands out when the environment becomes quiet. At night, there may be fewer external sounds, fewer tasks, and less social distraction. The brain can begin scanning for the ringing, buzzing, or hissing, and that attention can make the sound feel more important. This is one reason soft, steady background sound can be helpful at bedtime.

section_header: Why trying harder to sleep can backfire
audio_label: Why trying harder to sleep can backfire
audio_transcript: Sleep is unusual because effort does not always help. Trying to force sleep can make your mind more alert, especially if you start checking the clock, measuring the night, or predicting how bad tomorrow will be. The goal is not to work harder at sleeping. The goal is to create conditions where sleep is more likely to happen naturally.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Sleep drive: your body’s pressure for sleep
audio_label: Sleep drive: your body’s pressure for sleep
audio_transcript: Sleep drive is the natural pressure for sleep that builds the longer you are awake. When people spend too much time in bed awake, nap excessively, or go to bed much earlier to make up for a poor night, that pressure can weaken. A stronger sleep drive can make sleep more continuous and less fragile.

section_header: When the bed becomes a place for frustration
audio_label: When the bed becomes a place for frustration
audio_transcript: If you lie awake night after night, the bed can start to feel connected with frustration, worry, clock-checking, and tinnitus monitoring. Your brain may learn that bed means wakefulness instead of sleep. Stimulus control is a behavioral sleep idea designed to rebuild the connection between bed and successful sleep.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: In sleep treatment, stimulus control often means going to bed when sleepy, leaving bed if you are awake for a while, doing something quiet and relaxing, and returning when sleepiness returns. The point is not punishment, and it is not a test of willpower. It is a way of helping the brain relearn that bed is for sleep, not for hours of struggling.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Sleep thoughts can raise the alarm
audio_label: Sleep thoughts can raise the alarm
audio_transcript: Sleep-related thoughts can become convincing at night. Thoughts like “If I do not sleep eight hours, tomorrow is ruined” or “I will never fall asleep with tinnitus” can raise anxiety and make the body more alert. These thoughts may feel true in the moment, but they can often be checked and softened.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Sleep myths create pressure. You may hear that everyone needs exactly eight hours, that one bad night ruins the next day, or that staying in bed awake will eventually force sleep. A more balanced view is usually more helpful: sleep needs vary, bad nights happen, and your body can often function better than your anxious mind predicts.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Examples of sleep myths include: “I must get eight hours or I will fail,” “I can always catch up on weekends,” “alcohol helps me sleep better,” “complete silence is best,” “if I stay in bed long enough I will force sleep,” and “more time in bed always means more rest.” Each of these has a more balanced version that lowers pressure.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Sound can help at night by reducing the contrast between silence and tinnitus. The sound should usually be low-level, steady, and comfortable. Loud, surprising, or highly varied sound may keep the brain more alert. The goal is not to create a perfect sound environment. The goal is to make the night feel less stark and less tinnitus-focused.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

section_header: Sleep hygiene is helpful, but it is not the whole answer
audio_label: Sleep hygiene is helpful, but it is not the whole answer
audio_transcript: Sleep hygiene includes habits that support sleep: a consistent schedule, a calmer wind-down, less late caffeine, a comfortable bedroom, and fewer stimulating activities right before bed. These habits matter, but sleep hygiene alone may not fix insomnia. For many people, the bigger shift comes from changing the thoughts and behaviors that keep the bed connected with stress.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: A consistent sleep schedule helps your body clock predict when sleep and wakefulness should happen. A regular wake time is especially important, even after a rough night. This does not mean you must be rigid forever. It means giving your body repeated cues so the sleep system has a clearer rhythm.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: A wind-down routine gives the brain a transition. Reading, gentle stretching, quiet breathing, or calming audio can help signal that the day is ending. Try to avoid stressful work, intense conversations, or stimulating tasks right before bed when possible. The purpose is not to force sleep, but to lower the activation level around bedtime.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: A bedroom that is cool, dark, comfortable, and low in disruption can make sleep easier. For tinnitus, “quiet” does not always mean silent. A soft, steady sound can be useful if silence makes tinnitus stand out. Try to keep the bed connected mainly with sleep, so your brain has a clear signal about what the space is for.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Caffeine and nicotine can make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, especially later in the day. Alcohol may feel relaxing at first, but it can fragment sleep later in the night. Heavy meals close to bedtime can be disruptive for some people. Regular movement can support sleep, while intense late workouts may be too activating for some.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: If worries or to-do lists flood in at night, try giving them another place to go earlier in the evening. Some people write down worries, next steps, or tomorrow’s tasks before the wind-down begins. Breathing, mindfulness, or paired muscle relaxation can also help the body shift out of problem-solving mode.
playback_behavior: Manual next; stop at end. Autoplay optional in settings and default off.

audio_transcript: Stimulus control is the idea of rebuilding the connection between bed and sleep. Sleep drive is the pressure for sleep that builds while you are awake. Sleep distortions are rigid or threatening thoughts about sleep. Sleep hygiene is the set of habits and environmental choices that support healthier sleep.

audio_transcript: Start with one or two realistic changes rather than trying everything at once.
